text: Two worked examples are behind you. This lesson hands you a new scenario and asks you to design the approval process yourself, using the same method.

Mill Creek Design Studio, a fictional architecture firm, has a Time-Off Request object. HR's complaint: requests over five consecutive days get approved by whoever sees the email first -- sometimes a peer, not a manager -- and it's caused two scheduling conflicts this quarter.

Your job: write the entry criteria, design the approval step or steps, decide whether the record should lock while pending, write the final actions, and document the whole thing with Lesson 13's five-question template.

Check your own work against this list. Entry criteria that only catches requests over five days. One named approver tier. A locking decision that's actually justified. Both final actions written out. All five documentation questions answered.

Watch for the most common first-draft mistake: entry criteria written as 'more than zero days,' which routes even a single sick day into the same queue HR wanted reserved for longer requests. Re-read your criteria against the actual complaint.
A design that passes this checklist still isn't proven to work -- next lesson covers how to actually test it before it goes live.
